summary: This informational RFC overviews the Operations, Administration and Maintenance (OAM) toolset for MPLS-based transport networks. It covers fault management and performance monitoring in the data plane, as required by RFC 5860.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a guide to the tools for checking that a network line works and finding what broke.

how to monitor mpls transport networks
what is the generic associated channel
how do i measure packet loss in mpls-tp
subtitle: A guide to the toolset for monitoring and managing MPLS-based transport networks.

tldr.problem: Transport networks using MPLS need comprehensive fault detection, performance monitoring, and diagnostic tools operating in the data plane to support strict service level agreements.
tldr.mechanism: This document describes an OAM toolset built on extended versions of existing MPLS tools like BFD and LSP ping, plus new protocols for alarm reporting and performance measurement, all using a common in-band control channel.
tldr.outcome: Operators have a modular, interoperable set of tools for continuity checking, connectivity verification, defect reporting, loss and delay measurement, and diagnostics in MPLS transport networks.

today: RFC 6669 is an Informational RFC that provides an overview of MPLS-TP OAM. It remains the primary reference for understanding the comprehensive OAM toolset for MPLS transport networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) adapts MPLS for use in carrier transport networks, which demand high reliability and strict Service Level Agreements. This document provides an overview of the Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) toolset built for MPLS-TP. The toolset consists of fault management and performance monitoring capabilities that run in the data plane at different hierarchical levels (LSPs, Pseudowires, and MPLS Sections).

The OAM solution is based on three key principles: it reuses existing MPLS technology where possible, provides operational experience similar to traditional transport networks, and maintains full interoperability with existing MPLS OAM tools. The actual protocol specifications for each OAM tool are in separate RFCs; this document serves as a roadmap.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS is a way to send data through networks. This explains all the tools for checking that those paths are working, finding broken ones, and measuring quality.

sections.title: OAM Infrastructure
sections.content:
All MPLS-TP OAM packets run in-band, traveling with the data traffic they monitor and sharing the same fate. This in-band approach is achieved through the Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh), defined in RFC 5586. The G-ACh provides a common control channel that multiplexes transparently over LSPs and Sections.

OAM packets are identified by the Generic Association Label (GAL), a reserved MPLS label value. A Channel Type field in the Associated Channel Header (ACH) specifies which OAM protocol is being used, and each protocol has an IANA-assigned channel type. This common infrastructure allows all OAM functions to operate independently of the control or management plane, enabling basic OAM to function even in networks with no IP connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: OAM messages hitch a ride with the real data in special labeled packets. A label tells the router what kind of OAM message it is, so the router knows whether to check the path, measure delay, or report a problem.

sections.title: Fault Management Functions
sections.content:
The toolset provides both proactive and on-demand fault detection. Continuity Check and Connectivity Verification (CC-CV) functions continuously monitor paths for loss of continuity and unintended connections, using Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) messages at operator-configurable intervals (typically 100 ms for performance monitoring, 1 s for fault management). LSP ping provides on-demand connectivity verification.

Remote Defect Indication (RDI) allows an end point to report to its peer that a defect exists on a bidirectional path. Alarm Indication Signal (AIS) messages propagate from intermediate points to end points when a fault is detected at a server layer. Lock Instruct and Lock Reporting functions enable administrative control: an operator can lock a path for maintenance, or intermediate points can report an administrative lock condition. Route Tracing on-demand identifies intermediate points along a path, and Diagnostic tests include data-plane loopback for testing connectivity to intermediate nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Proactive tools continuously check that a path is still alive. When something breaks, the tools can tell both ends of the path, suppress false alarms, lock a path for work, and trace where the problem is.

sections.title: Performance Monitoring
sections.content:
The toolset includes standardized protocols for measuring network quality. Packet Loss Measurement (LM) allows operators to quantify the packet loss ratio by having end points exchange counters of transmitted and received messages within a bounded time period. The protocol supports both direct measurement (using data-plane counters) and inferred mode (using test messages). It measures loss in both directions using a simple query/response model.

Packet Delay Measurement (DM) quantifies one-way and two-way transmission delays. DM uses timestamps (IEEE 1588 by default, but also supports NTP) and can vary message sizes to measure delays for different packet sizes. From loss and delay measurements, operators can derive throughput and delay variation metrics. All measurement protocols use the same G-ACh infrastructure and support both continuous and on-demand modes.
sections.plainLanguage: Performance tools measure how many packets are lost and how long messages take to cross the network. Networks use these measurements to report on service quality to customers.

sections.title: Practical Deployment
sections.content:
In practice, CC-CV and Link Down Indication (LDI) work together for fast failure detection. Operators can run CC-CV at a slower rate (longer BFD intervals) and rely on LDI to trigger rapid protection switching when a failure occurs at a server layer. Diagnostic tests and loopback functions support associated and co-routed bidirectional LSPs, as well as multi-segment pseudowires. Lock Reporting helps distinguish administrative maintenance from actual defects, enabling alarm suppression above the point of the lock.

The modular design allows operators to deploy different subsets of functions according to their network needs and requirements. All functions support point-to-point paths that span single or multiple domains, with some functions also supporting point-to-multipoint LSPs and unidirectional paths when a return path exists.
sections.plainLanguage: Network operators pick which tools to use based on their needs. Some want to detect failures fast, others need to measure performance, and some need to lock down a path for maintenance while keeping the network running.
